  • casts such as float(amount), integer(code), str(code), and datetime(ts)
  • aggregate aliases such as avg(amount) -> mean
  • weighted mean aliases wavg and wmean -> weighted_mean
  • arity-dependent min / max
  • unknown bare calls as backend-function candidates, for example log(price)

Known function arity is validated by the normalizer. Public parser attachment remains best-effort: invalid or unsupported semantic forms get expression_ir: null rather than breaking existing raw-string execution.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
Stage 3 does not:

  • change pandas, Polars, DuckDB, or SQL generation
  • validate column existence
  • decide backend capability support
  • parse comparison conditions into expression IR
  • define a complete program IR

docs.title: Status And Scope
docs.text:
This document defines the boundary between Pivotal assignment syntax and backend-independent expression handling.

The migration is deliberately additive:

  • The statement parser continues to capture assignment expressions as strings.
  • DSLParser.parse() continues to return the existing public syntax AST.
  • Assignment nodes retain their public expression string unchanged.
  • Supported assignment expressions also receive additive expression_ast and expression_ir fields.
  • Backend generators consume expression_ir for the migrated assignment subsets: basic arithmetic, scalar functions, casts, and aggregates. Unsupported nodes continue using the raw expression fallback.

This document defines expression and condition nodes only. It does not define a complete program IR or change expression semantics.

docs.title: Compiler Boundary
docs.text:
The intended compiler pipeline is:

Pivotal source
  -> statement parser
  -> public syntax AST
  -> compile-time expansion and column-loop lowering
  -> standalone expression parser
  -> additive expression AST
  -> additive semantic normalization
  -> IR-first backend generation with legacy fallback

Expression parsing happens after compile-time function/value expansion and column-loop lowering. This ensures the expression AST describes the assignment that backend generators actually receive.

docs.title: Initial Expression Language
docs.text:
Stage 1 recognizes:

  • Column references: price
  • Integer and float literals: 1, 0.5, 1e3
  • String literals using single or double quotes
  • Boolean literals: true, false (case-insensitive)
  • Null literals: null, none (case-insensitive)
  • Parentheses
  • Unary + and -
  • Binary +, -, *, /, %, and **
  • Generic function calls: upper(name), log(price)
  • Runtime references: :multiplier
  • Runtime calls: :clean_name(name)

Operator precedence, from highest to lowest, is:

  1. Parenthesized expressions, literals, references, and calls
  2. Power ** (right-associative)
  3. Unary + and -
  4. Multiply, divide, and modulo
  5. Add and subtract

Parentheses affect tree structure but are not retained as separate nodes.

The initial expression parser does not recognize conditions, attribute access, subscripts, lists, dictionaries, keyword arguments, or arbitrary Python expressions.

docs.title: Node Vocabulary
docs.text:
All expression nodes are JSON-serializable dictionaries.

Column reference:

{"kind": "column", "name": "price"}

Literal:

{"kind": "literal", "literal_type": "float", "value": 0.1}

literal_type is one of integer, float, string, boolean, or null. Null literals have a JSON null value.

Unary operation:

{
  "kind": "unary",
  "operator": "negative",
  "operand": {"kind": "column", "name": "amount"}
}

Binary operation:

{
  "kind": "binary",
  "operator": "multiply",
  "left": {"kind": "column", "name": "price"},
  "right": {"kind": "column", "name": "quantity"}
}

Binary operator names are add, subtract, multiply, divide, modulo, and power. Unary operator names are positive and negative.

Generic function call:

{
  "kind": "call",
  "name": "upper",
  "arguments": [{"kind": "column", "name": "name"}]
}

Runtime reference and runtime call:

{"kind": "runtime_reference", "name": "multiplier"}

{
  "kind": "runtime_call",
  "name": "clean_name",
  "arguments": [{"kind": "column", "name": "name"}]
}

docs.title: Function Semantics
docs.text:
Stage 1 records generic bare calls without deciding their meaning. Stage 3 semantic normalization distinguishes:

  • Pivotal built-in scalar functions such as upper(name)
  • Pivotal aggregate functions such as mean(amount)
  • Arity-dependent functions such as aggregate max(amount) versus scalar max(amount, 0)
  • Backend-native functions such as log(price)

Runtime calls have a separate node kind because :clean_name(name) explicitly requests a host Python callable. Runtime references are also distinct from columns.

Compile-time references do not have an expression node kind in Stage 1. Compile-time values are expanded before expression parsing, so the expression parser sees the resulting literal, column, or expression text.

docs.title: Fallback And Compatibility Policy
docs.text:
Expression parsing is best-effort during this migration.

For a supported expression, an assignment node is additive:

{
  "type": "assign",
  "expression": "price * quantity",
  "expression_ast": {
    "kind": "binary",
    "operator": "multiply",
    "left": {"kind": "column", "name": "price"},
    "right": {"kind": "column", "name": "quantity"}
  },
  "expression_ir": {
    "kind": "binary",
    "operator": "multiply",
    "left": {"kind": "column", "name": "price"},
    "right": {"kind": "column", "name": "quantity"}
  }
}

For an unsupported legacy expression, expression_ast and expression_ir are null and the raw expression string remains authoritative. Unsupported expression syntax must not turn a previously valid Pivotal program into a parse failure.

Backend generators may consume explicitly migrated expression_ir subsets. Unsupported nodes must fall back to the raw expression string so current pandas, Polars, DuckDB, and SQL behavior is preserved outside migrated slices.

docs.title: Condition IR Metadata
docs.text:
Condition-bearing syntax nodes receive best-effort condition metadata. The existing public conditions, operators, and query_str fields are retained for compatibility and as the fallback for unsupported condition shapes.

Condition-bearing nodes receive additive fields:

{
  "condition_ast": {
    "kind": "predicate",
    "operator": "greater_than",
    "left": {"kind": "column", "name": "amount"},
    "right": {"kind": "literal", "literal_type": "integer", "value": 100}
  },
  "condition_ir": {
    "kind": "predicate",
    "operator": "greater_than",
    "left": {"kind": "column", "name": "amount"},
    "right": {"kind": "literal", "literal_type": "integer", "value": 100}
  }
}

Multiple conditions are represented as left-associative logical nodes:

{
  "kind": "logical",
  "operator": "and",
  "left": {"kind": "predicate"},
  "right": {"kind": "predicate"}
}

Predicate operands reuse the expression node vocabulary where possible: columns, literals, and runtime references. Condition-specific collection and reference operands use list, list_reference, and compile_reference nodes.

Stage 7 attaches condition metadata after compile-time expansion and column-loop lowering. Unsupported condition metadata must produce null condition fields rather than turning a previously valid Pivotal program into a parse failure.

Stage 8 lets backend condition emitters consume supported condition_ir nodes for filters, condition-based data-quality rules, conditional assignments, and case branches. If condition_ir is absent or contains an unsupported node, the emitters fall back to the legacy conditions and operators fields.

Stage 8 does not change the public syntax AST, accepted syntax, or backend surface behavior. It only moves the supported condition codegen subset onto the structured predicate/logical metadata.

docs.title: Semantic IR Node Vocabulary
docs.text:
Stage 3 adds semantic nodes for known expression meaning.

Scalar function:

{
  "kind": "scalar_function",
  "function": "upper",
  "arguments": [{"kind": "column", "name": "name"}]
}

Aggregate:

{
  "kind": "aggregate",
  "function": "mean",
  "arguments": [{"kind": "column", "name": "amount"}]
}

Cast:

{
  "kind": "cast",
  "target_type": "float",
  "expression": {"kind": "column", "name": "amount"}
}

Backend function candidate:

{
  "kind": "backend_function",
  "name": "log",
  "arguments": [{"kind": "column", "name": "price"}]
}

The Stage 3 function registry normalizes aliases and arity-dependent functions:

  • avg(amount) -> aggregate mean
  • wavg(amount, weight) and wmean(amount, weight) -> aggregate weighted_mean
  • float(amount), integer(code), str(code), and datetime(ts) -> cast
  • max(amount) and min(amount) -> aggregate maximum and minimum
  • max(amount, 0) and min(amount, 0) -> scalar greatest and least
  • unknown bare calls such as log(price) -> backend_function

Known function arity is validated by the normalizer. Public parser attachment remains best-effort: if semantic normalization fails, expression_ir is null and raw-string execution remains authoritative.

docs.title: Source Locations
docs.text:
Future expression nodes may receive an optional source object:

{
  "source": {
    "start_offset": 12,
    "end_offset": 28,
    "line": 3,
    "column": 9,
    "end_line": 3,
    "end_column": 25
  }
}

Offsets are zero-based and end-exclusive. Lines and columns are one-based. Locations should refer to the original Pivotal source when available.

Stage 1 does not attach locations because expression parsing currently occurs after compile-time expansion and loop lowering, where generated expressions do not always have a direct original-source span.

docs.title: Deferred Decisions
docs.text:
The following are intentionally deferred:

  • Complete program IR and schema versioning
  • Backend capability validation
  • Backend generation from unsupported expression nodes
  • Backend generation from unsupported condition nodes
  • Substrait lowering

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
Pivotal is a line-oriented pipeline language. Each statement occupies one or more lines, sub-options are indented beneath their parent, and operations flow top-to-bottom.

For exact command forms and accepted options, see the Syntax Reference.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
A Pivotal script is a sequence of blocks. Each block begins with a top-level statement (load, with, save, delete) and its indented sub-statements:

load "data/sales.csv" as sales      # top-level: load a file

with sales as summary             # top-level: define a table
    filter status == "active"     # indented: sub-operation
    group by region               #           sub-operation
        agg sum revenue as total  #           sub-option of group by
    sort total desc               # back to with level

save package as "output/report"   # top-level: save output

docs.title: Indentation
docs.text: Indentation is significant but flexible — any consistent number of spaces or tabs works. Sub-options must be indented relative to their parent; they end when the indentation returns to the parent level.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
# Single-line comment (hash)

-- Single-line comment (SQL style)

/* Multi-line
   comment */

docs.title: Python variable references
docs.text:
Prefix a Python variable name with : to reference it from the surrounding scope:

threshold = 500
categories = ["A", "B"]

with sales as filtered
    filter amount > :threshold
    filter category in :categories

load :my_file_path as data

This works in Jupyter (referencing notebook variables) and in the Python API (referencing the namespace passed to execute()).

docs.title: String quoting
docs.text:
Strings use double quotes:

filter name == "Alice"
load "path/to/file.csv" as data

docs.title: Statements
docs.text: Statement Purpose load Load a file into a table with Set or create a table filter Filter rows list / scalar / dict Define reusable values and config assert / check Validate data quality select Keep specific columns drop Remove specific columns distinct Remove duplicate rows assign Create or modify columns for Apply column operations across multiple columns function Define reusable pipeline functions cast Cast a column to a different type rename Rename columns sort Sort rows group by Aggregate by groups agg Aggregate over all rows (no grouping) merge Join two tables pivot Pivot to wide format unpivot Pivot to long format rank Rank rows lag / lead Shift values cumsum etc. Cumulative statistics rolling Rolling window statistics fillna Fill missing values dropna Drop rows with missing values concat Stack tables vertically python Embed Python code apply Apply a Python function to a table show Display inline plot Create a chart pivot plot Create a chart with aggregation table Create a publication-ready table save Export tables and charts delete Remove a table from memory

docs.title: Syntax Reference
docs.text: This page is a compact reference for Pivotal statements and options. It is intended for checking exact command shapes; see the user guide topic pages for longer examples and explanation.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Placeholder Meaning <table> Pivotal table/DataFrame name <col> Column name <name> Identifier used for a table, column, chart, function, or native value <value> Boolean, number, string, identifier, path, None, or Python variable <expr> Raw expression text parsed by the selected backend <condition> One or more comparisons joined by and or or :var / :func(col) Python runtime variable or callable [ ... ] Optional syntax in this reference, unless shown inside code as a list

Pivotal identifiers start with a letter and may contain letters, numbers, and underscores. Strings may use single or double quotes. Comments may use #, --, or /* ... */.

docs.title: Values, Lists, and Conditions
docs.text:
Accepted value forms:

True
False
None
123
-123
12.5
"text"
'text'
identifier
:python_variable
:python_list[0]
:python_dict["key"]
path/to/file.csv

Accepted list forms:

[a, b, c]
(a, b, c)
a, b, c

Conditions use a column on the left:

<col> == <value>
<col> != <value>
<col> > <value>
<col> < <value>
<col> >= <value>
<col> <= <value>
<col> between [<low>, <high>]
<col> contains <value>
<col> not contains <value>
<col> matches <value>
<col> not matches <value>
<col> startswith <value>
<col> endswith <value>
<col> in <list-or-name-or-python-var>
<col> not in <list-or-name-or-python-var>

Multiple conditions may be joined with and or or.

docs.title: list
docs.text:
Define a reusable list:

list <name> = <value>, ...

List values may be literals, identifiers, paths, or Python variables. Named lists can be used in column lists, filter value lists, loop sources, and function arguments.

Index into a known list with square brackets:

list limits = -5, 5

with sales
    filter zscore > limits[0] and zscore < limits[1]

docs.title: scalar
docs.text:
Define a reusable single value:

scalar <name> = <value>

Examples:

scalar gst = 0.1
scalar cutoff = :python_cutoff

docs.title: dict
docs.text:
Define a nested dictionary inline:

dict <name>
    <key> = <value>, ...
    <key>: <value>, ...
    <nested_key>
        <key> = <value>

Load a dictionary from JSON or YAML:

dict <name> from "<path>.json"
dict <name> from "<path>.yml"
dict <name> from "<path>.yaml"

Bind an existing Python dictionary:

dict <name> = :python_dict

Access known dictionary values with dot paths:

config.thresholds.high
config.columns.money

Native values persist in the Python namespace. Later cells may also use :name, :name[0], or :name["key"] runtime references, but native lookup is preferred inside Pivotal code when the value belongs to the pipeline.

docs.title: load
docs.text:
Load a file into a table:

load <path-or-string-or-python-var> as <table>
load <path-or-string-or-python-var> as <table>
    <reader_option> <value>
    <reader_option> = <value>
    <reader_option> [<value>, ...]

Examples:

load "sales.csv" as sales
load :input_path as sales
load "sales.csv" as sales
    header 0
    sep ";"

load reader options are pass-through keyword arguments for the generated file reader. CSV files use read_csv, Excel files use read_excel, and Parquet files use read_parquet.

Load tables from the active package:

load all
load <table>

docs.title: bulk load
docs.text:
Load a list or folder of CSV or Parquet files.

bulk load :files as <table>
bulk load "<folder>" as <table>
bulk load "<file1>", "<file2>" as <table>
bulk load :files as <table1>, <table2>, ...
bulk load :files as :aliases
bulk load :files as <table>
    source column <col>
    source value path|filename|stem
    <reader_option> <value>

With one static alias, files are concatenated into one table and a source column is added. With multiple aliases, or with a Python alias list, each file is loaded as a separate table.

Folder sources are expanded in sorted filename order. A folder must be non-empty and contain only CSV files or only Parquet files.

Defaults:

Option Default source column source source value filename

docs.title: from
docs.text:
Load tables or query results from a database.

from <database-path-or-uri-or-python-var>
    load <sql_table> as <table>, ...
    query "<sql>" as <table>

The block may contain any mix of load and query lines. Supported source forms include SQLite paths, DuckDB paths, SQLAlchemy URIs, and Python variables containing those values.

docs.title: with
docs.text:
Set the active table:

with <table>

Create a derived table and make it active:

with <source_table> as <new_table>

Statements that transform a table are normally indented under with.

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:
Create or replace a column on the active table:

<target_col> = <expr>

Conditional assignment:

<target_col> = <expr>
    where <condition>
    else <expr>

Grouped/windowed assignment:

<target_col> = <expr>
    by <col>, ...

Multi-case assignment:

<target_col> =
    where <condition>; <expr>
    where <condition>: <expr>
    else <expr>

map can be used instead of where as an alias in multi-case assignment.

The else branch is optional. Without it, unmatched rows receive the backend's missing value.

Python runtime functions in assignment expressions must use ::

<target_col> = :python_func(<col>)

Bare function calls are reserved for built-in Pivotal functions and backend-native functions.

docs.title: for
docs.text:
Repeat column-oriented operations over a list of columns.

for <loop_var> in <col>, ...
    <loop_var> = <expr>

for <loop_var> in :python_column_list
    <loop_var> = <expr>

Inside a for block, assignment targets can be built from identifiers and string literals:

for col in price, cost
    col + "_clean" = col

Allowed statements inside for are assignment, cast, fillna, drop, dropna, round, rank, lag, lead, cumsum, cummean, cummin, cummax, and rolling.

docs.title: filter
docs.text:
Keep rows matching a condition:

filter <condition>

docs.title: assert and check
docs.text:
Validate data quality. assert fails on invalid data; check warns and continues.

assert <condition>
check <condition>
assert <col>, ... unique
check <col>, ... unique
assert <col>, ... not null
check <col>, ... not null

docs.title: select
docs.text:
Keep selected columns:

select <col>, ...
select <col> as <new_col>, ...
select :python_column_or_columns
select matches "<regex>"

Aliases are supported for explicit column names. A Python variable may provide a single column or a list of columns.

End a physical line with \ to continue a long Pivotal statement:

select customer_id, product, region, \
    revenue, quantity, date

docs.title: drop
docs.text:
Remove columns:

drop <col>, ...
drop matches "<regex>"

docs.title: rename
docs.text:
Rename columns:

rename <old_col> as <new_col>, ...

docs.title: sort / order by
docs.text:
Sort rows:

sort <col> [asc|desc], ...
order by <col> [asc|desc], ...
sort :python_column_or_columns [asc|desc]

Ascending order is the default.

docs.title: distinct
docs.text:
Drop duplicate rows:

distinct
distinct <col>, ...

Without columns, duplicates are checked across the full row.

docs.title: fillna
docs.text:
Fill missing values:

fillna <value>
fillna <col> <value>, <col> <value>, ...
fillna
    <col> = <value>
    <col> = <value>

docs.title: dropna
docs.text:
Drop rows with missing values:

dropna
dropna <col>, ...

docs.title: cast
docs.text:
Cast one or more columns:

cast <col>, ... as int|integer|float|string|str|bool|boolean|datetime [strict]

Without strict, bad values are coerced where the backend supports coercion.

docs.title: round
docs.text:
Round numeric columns:

round <col>, ... <decimals>
round <col> <decimals> as <new_col>

The as form is valid only with a single source column.

docs.title: group by
docs.text:
Group and aggregate the active table:

group by <col-or-python-var>, ...
    agg <agg_item>, ...

If agg is omitted, backends use their default grouped aggregation behavior.

docs.title: agg
docs.text:
Aggregate the whole active table without grouping:

agg <agg_item>, ...

Aggregation item forms:

<func> <col-or-python-var> [as <new_col>]
<func>(<col-or-python-var>) [as <new_col>]
quantile <col-or-python-var> <q> [as <new_col>]
quantile(<col-or-python-var>, <q>) [as <new_col>]
percentile <col-or-python-var> <p> [as <new_col>]
percentile(<col-or-python-var>, <p>) [as <new_col>]
wmean(<col-or-python-var>, <weight-col-or-python-var>) [as <new_col>]
wmean <weight-col-or-python-var> <col-or-python-var> [as <new_col>]
wmean <weight-col-or-python-var> <col1> <col2> ...
:python_func <col> ... [as <new_col>]
:python_func(<col>, ..., <kw>=<value>) [as <new_col>]

Built-in aggregation functions accepted by the grammar are mean, avg, sum, min, max, count, median, std, nunique, quantile, and percentile.

Older wavg syntax is accepted as a backward-compatible alias for wmean, but new code should use wmean.

Pivotal also expands shorthand such as:

agg mean price, cost

to:

agg mean price, mean cost

docs.title: pivot
docs.text:
Create a pivot table:

pivot
    rows <col-or-python-var>, ...
    cols <col-or-python-var>, ...
    agg <agg_item>, ...

rows, cols, and agg lines may appear in any order. Use the same aggregation item forms as group by.

docs.title: unpivot
docs.text:
Convert wide data to long data:

unpivot
    id <col-or-python-var>, ...
    cols <col-or-python-var>, ...
    variable "<variable_column_name>"
    value "<value_column_name>"

Defaults:

Option Default variable variable value value

docs.title: merge
docs.text:
Join another table to the active table:

merge <right_table>
<left|right|inner|outer> merge <right_table>
merge <right_table> on <key>, ...
<left|right|inner|outer> merge <right_table> on <key>, ...
    <merge_option> <value>
    <merge_option> = <value>

The default merge type is inner. Indented merge options are pass-through keyword arguments for the generated backend merge/join call.

docs.title: concat
docs.text:
Append tables vertically to the active table:

concat <table>, ...

docs.title: intersect
docs.text:
Keep rows in the active table that also appear in the listed tables:

intersect <table>, ...

docs.title: exclude
docs.text:
Remove rows from the active table that appear in the listed tables:

exclude <table>, ...

docs.title: rank
docs.text:
Rank rows by a column:

rank <col> [asc|desc] [pct] as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...

Ascending order is the default. pct returns percentile ranks.

docs.title: lag and lead
docs.text:
Read values from prior or later rows:

lag <col> <periods> as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...
    order <col>

lead <col> <periods> as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...
    order <col>

Use order to make the row order explicit.

docs.title: Cumulative functions
docs.text:
Compute cumulative values:

cumsum <col> as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...
    order <col>

cummean <col> as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...
    order <col>

cummin <col> as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...
    order <col>

cummax <col> as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...
    order <col>

docs.title: rolling
docs.text:
Compute rolling-window values:

rolling <agg_func> <col> <window_size> as <new_col>
    by <col>, ...
    order <col>
    min_periods [=] <n>

Rolling aggregation functions use the same grammar token as agg: mean, avg, sum, min, max, count, median, std, and nunique. Backend support for individual rolling functions may vary.

docs.title: show
docs.text:
Display the active table:

show
show head
show summary
show shape
show columns

docs.title: plot
docs.text:
Create or update a matplotlib chart:

plot <name>
plot <kind> <name>
plot <kind> on <existing_chart_name>
plot <name>
    <plot_option> <value>
    <plot_option> = <value>
    <plot_option> [<value>, ...]
    by <col>
    cols <n>
    show

Common plot options include kind, x, y, title, legend, c, colormap, style, and canvas. Most options are passed through to pandas or matplotlib plotting code.

Labels can be supplied after a value:

plot line sales_chart
    x month "Month"
    y revenue "Revenue"

docs.title: pivot plot
docs.text:
Group, aggregate, and plot in one command:

pivot plot <name>
pivot plot <kind> <name>
    x <col> ["label"]
    y <func> <col>, <func> <col>, ... ["label"]
    by <col>
    cols <n>
    canvas <name>
    show

docs.title: table
docs.text:
Create a Great Tables table:

table <name>
    title "<text>"
    subtitle "<text>"
    font size <number>
    font "<family>"
    stub <col>
    stub <col> "<label>"
    stub <col>, <group_col>
    stub <col>, <group_col> "<label>"
    stripe
    canvas <name>
    label <col> as "<label>", ...
    format <col> as <format_type>
    format <format_type>
    style "<path>"
    summary <summary_spec>, ...
    spanner <col>, ... "<label>"
    auto spanner
    show

Format types:

number
number <decimals>
integer
currency
currency <code>
percent
percent <decimals>
date

Summary specs:

<func>
<func> as "<label>"

docs.title: python
docs.text:
Run a single Python statement:

python <python-code>

Run a Python block:

python
    <python-code>
end

python...end blocks are preprocessed into a single Python statement before parsing, so comments and indentation inside the Python code are preserved.

docs.title: apply
docs.text:
Apply a Python function to the active table:

apply :<python_function_name>

The function receives the active DataFrame and must return a DataFrame.

docs.title: save
docs.text:
Save outputs to a Pivotal data package:

save package as "<directory>/<package_name>"
save package as :python_path
    format <csv|parquet>
    chart_format <png|svg>
    include <name>, ...
    exclude <name>, ...

Save one table to a path or managed catalog table:

save <table> as "<path>"
save <table> as :python_path
save <table> as table "<catalog>.<schema>.<table>"

File formats are inferred from the path suffix. Managed table support depends on the selected backend.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
Remove a table from the session namespace:

delete <table>

docs.title: function
docs.text:
Define a reusable non-recursive pipeline:

function <name>([<param>, <param>=<default>, ...])
    <statement>
    <statement>
    return <name>, ...

return is optional. It records output metadata for Python-callable wrappers.

docs.title: Function calls
docs.text:
Call a Pivotal pipeline function:

<function_name>(<arg>, <arg>, <keyword>=<arg>, ...)

Function arguments may be values, Python variables, named lists, or inline round-bracket lists:

clean_sales(raw, clean, (price, cost), min_amount=:threshold)

docs.title: Data Quality
docs.text:
assert and check validate the active table without changing its rows or columns.

Use assert for rules that must pass. If any row violates the rule, Pivotal raises an AssertionError and stops execution.

Use check for softer rules. If any row violates the rule, Pivotal emits a UserWarning and continues.

with orders
    assert order_id unique
    assert customer_id not null
    assert status in ["open", "closed", "cancelled"]
    check amount >= 0

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
assert and check accept the same condition syntax as filter:

with sales
    assert amount >= 0
    assert status in ["open", "closed"]
    check discount <= amount
    check region not in ["test", "sandbox"]

docs.title: Shorthand Rules
docs.text:
Use unique to validate key columns:

with orders
    assert order_id unique
    assert order_id, line_id unique

Use not null to require values:

with orders
    assert customer_id not null
    check shipped_at not null

docs.title: Backend Notes
docs.text:
The pandas, Polars, and DuckDB backends evaluate data-quality commands at runtime.

The SQL CTE backend emits skipped comments for assert and check commands, because plain SQL export cannot raise Python exceptions or emit Python warnings.

docs.title: load — load a file
docs.text:
Load a CSV, Excel, or Parquet file into a named table.

load "<file_path>" as <table_name>

load "data/sales.csv" as sales
load "catalog.xlsx" as products
load "archive.parquet" as transactions

Use a Python variable for the path:

load :my_file_path as data

docs.title: bulk load - load generated file lists
docs.text:
Load many CSV or Parquet files from a Python list or folder. With one alias, Pivotal concatenates the files into one table and adds a source column containing the input filename.

files = ["data/jan.csv", "data/feb.csv", "data/mar.csv"]

bulk load :files as sales
bulk load "data/monthly" as sales

The concat mode unions columns by name, so files with extra or missing columns are combined with missing values where needed.

When the source is a folder, files are loaded in sorted filename order. The folder must be non-empty and contain only CSV files or only Parquet files.

Customize the provenance column:

bulk load :files as sales
    source column file
    source value stem

source value can be filename, path, or stem.

Use multiple aliases to load each file separately:

bulk load :files as jan_sales, feb_sales, mar_sales

Or provide aliases from a Python list:

tables = ["jan_sales", "feb_sales", "mar_sales"]

bulk load :files as :tables

The file list and alias list must have the same length. Aliases must be valid Pivotal table identifiers.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Indent options beneath the load statement:

load "data/sales.csv" as sales
    header 0           # row index of header (default 0)
    names ["product", "quantity", "price"]  # override column names
Option Description header <n> Row index to use as column headers (default 0) names [...] List of column names to use instead of the file header

docs.title: Set active table
docs.text:
Make an existing table the active table for subsequent operations:

with sales
    filter price > 100
    sort price desc

docs.title: Create a derived table
docs.text:
Create a new table by applying operations to an existing one. The original is unchanged:

with sales as top_sales
    filter revenue > 1000
    sort revenue desc

with orders as summary
    group by region
        agg sum amount as total

Without as, operations apply to the named table in-place:

with sales              # operates on 'sales', modifying it
    filter active == True

With as, a new table is created:

with sales as active_sales    # creates 'active_sales', 'sales' unchanged
    filter active == True

docs.title: Chaining
docs.text:
Multiple with blocks can be chained — the output of one becomes the input of the next:

load "data.csv" as raw

with raw as cleaned
    dropna price, quantity
    fillna 0

with cleaned as summary
    group by category
        agg sum price as total
    sort total desc

docs.title: from — load from a database
docs.text:
Connect to a database and load one or more tables or query results into named DataFrames.

from "<database_path_or_uri>"
    load <sql_table> as <df_name>, ...
    query "<SQL string>" as <df_name>

docs.title: Load tables by name
docs.text:
from "data/mydb.sqlite"
    load orders as orders, customers as customers

Each load item reads the named SQL table with SELECT * FROM <table>. Multiple tables can be listed on a single line, comma-separated.

docs.title: Run arbitrary SQL
docs.text:
from "data/mydb.sqlite"
    query "SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE active = 1" as active_customers

docs.title: Mix load and query in one block
docs.text:
from "data/mydb.sqlite"
    load orders as orders_raw
    query "SELECT category, SUM(amount) as total FROM orders GROUP BY category" as summary

The connection is opened once and all reads share it.

docs.title: Supported sources
docs.text: Source Example path Notes SQLite "data/mydb.sqlite" Also .db, .sqlite3 DuckDB "data/warehouse.duckdb" Also .ddb Python variable :conn_str Variable must hold a path or URI PostgreSQL URI "postgresql://user:pass@host/db" Requires SQLAlchemy — see below MySQL URI "mysql+pymysql://user:pass@host/db" Requires SQLAlchemy + driver Other SQLAlchemy any dialect+driver://... URI Requires SQLAlchemy + driver

docs.title: SQLAlchemy support (PostgreSQL, MySQL, and others)
docs.text:
For databases other than SQLite and DuckDB, Pivotal uses SQLAlchemy as the connection layer. SQLAlchemy is a Python library that provides a unified interface to many databases via connection URI strings.

Install SQLAlchemy and a driver:

# PostgreSQL
pip install sqlalchemy psycopg2-binary

# MySQL
pip install sqlalchemy pymysql

# Microsoft SQL Server
pip install sqlalchemy pyodbc

Usage:

from "postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb"
    load products as products
    query "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'open'" as open_orders

If SQLAlchemy is not installed, Pivotal will raise a clear error with the install command rather than a cryptic import failure.

Polars backend: Uses connectorx for URI sources if available (faster), falling back to SQLAlchemy + pl.from_pandas(). Install with pip install connectorx.

DuckDB backend: Uses DuckDB's native extensions (postgres_scanner, etc.) for URI sources rather than SQLAlchemy.

docs.title: delete — remove a table
docs.text:
Remove a table from memory:

delete sales
delete temp_table

In Jupyter, this is equivalent to del sales in Python.

Tables must have compatible columns.

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
The filter statement keeps rows that match a condition. Rows that do not match are dropped.

with sales as active
    filter status == "active"

docs.title: Comparison operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning == Equal != Not equal > Greater than < Less than >= Greater than or equal <= Less than or equal 
filter price > 100
filter quantity != 0
filter status == "active"
filter score >= 0.9
filter discount <= 0.5

docs.title: Logical operators
docs.text:
Combine conditions with and / or:

filter amount > 1000 and category == "premium"
filter status == "active" or price > 500
filter region == "North" and status == "active" and amount > 100

Note

and binds more tightly than or. Use parentheses if you need explicit grouping — though in practice most filters are simple enough that this doesn't arise.

docs.title: Membership — in / not in
docs.text:
Test whether a value is in a list:

filter region in ["North", "South", "East"]
filter category not in ["test", "draft"]

Use a Python variable for the list:

valid_regions = ["North", "South"]

filter region in :valid_regions

docs.title: Range — between
docs.text:
Test whether a value falls within an inclusive range:

filter price between [100, 500]
filter score between [0.8, 1.0]

docs.title: String matching
docs.text:
Operator Meaning contains "x" String contains substring not contains "x" String does not contain substring matches "pattern" String matches regex pattern anywhere not matches "pattern" String does not match regex pattern startswith "x" String starts with prefix endswith "x" String ends with suffix 
filter product contains "Laptop"
filter name not contains "test"
filter email matches ".+@.+\\..+"
filter event startswith "login"
filter filename endswith ".csv"

Use ^ and $ anchors when the whole string must match the pattern.

docs.title: Python variable references
docs.text:
Any filter value can be a Python variable, prefixed with ::

min_price = 100
target_region = "North"

filter price > :min_price
filter region == :target_region

docs.title: Multiple filter lines
docs.text:
Multiple filter lines under the same with block are applied in sequence (AND logic):

with sales as result
    filter status == "active"
    filter amount > 500
    filter region in ["North", "South"]

docs.title: Lists and Functions
docs.text:
This page has been split into two focused topics:

  • Values: Scalars, Dicts, and Lists
  • Pipeline Control: Checks, Loops, and Functions

Use the values page for list, scalar, and dict syntax. Use the pipeline-control page for assert, check, for, function, and function calls.

docs.title: group by — aggregate by groups
docs.text:
Group rows by one or more columns and compute aggregate statistics. Each aggregation sub-clause is prefixed with agg:

with sales as summary
    group by region
        agg sum revenue as total

docs.title: Aggregation functions
docs.text:
Function Description sum Sum mean Arithmetic mean count Count of non-null values min Minimum max Maximum median Median std Standard deviation nunique Count of unique values quantile Quantile, with q from 0 to 1 percentile Percentile, with p from 0 to 100 wmean Weighted average

Both space and bracket syntax are accepted:

agg sum revenue as total              # space syntax
agg sum(revenue) as total             # bracket syntax — both are equivalent
agg quantile revenue 0.9 as p90       # quantile: value column first
agg percentile(revenue, 90) as p90    # percentile: value column first
agg wmean quantity price as avg       # space syntax: wmean weight_col value_col
agg wmean(price, quantity) as avg     # bracket syntax: wmean(value_col, weight_col)

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
with sales as by_region
    group by region
        agg sum revenue as total

with sales as by_category
    group by category
        agg mean price as avg_price

with events as counts
    group by event_type
        agg count id as n

docs.title: Multiple aggregations
docs.text:
List multiple aggregation functions separated by commas on a single agg line, or on multiple agg lines:

with sales as summary
    group by region
        agg sum revenue as total, mean revenue as avg, count id as deals

When the same aggregation function applies to several columns, you can write the function once:

with sales as averages
    group by region
        agg mean price, cost, margin

This is equivalent to agg mean price, mean cost, mean margin.

with sales as detailed
    group by region
        agg sum revenue as total
        agg mean revenue as avg_deal
        agg max revenue as top_deal
        agg count id as n_deals

docs.title: Multiple group-by columns
docs.text:
with sales as by_region_category
    group by region, category
        agg sum revenue as total, count id as deals

docs.title: Named results
docs.text:
The as <name> clause gives the aggregated column a name. Without it, Pivotal generates a name automatically:

agg sum revenue as total_revenue
agg count id as deal_count
agg mean price as avg_price

docs.title: Weighted average
docs.text:
wmean <weight_col> <value_col> computes a weighted mean. Note the argument order differs between the two syntaxes: space form takes weight first, bracket form takes value first.

with products
    group by category
        agg wmean quantity price as avg_price   # space: weight first
        agg wmean(price, quantity) as avg_price  # bracket: value first

wavg is accepted as a backward-compatible alias for wmean.

docs.title: Quantiles and percentiles
docs.text:
quantile <value_col> <q> uses a probability from 0 to 1. percentile <value_col> <p> is equivalent but uses 0 to 100.

with sales as thresholds
    group by product
        agg quantile revenue 0.9 as p90
        agg percentile(revenue, 95) as p95

docs.title: Custom Python aggregations
docs.text:
In pandas pipelines, prefix a Python function with : to use it in an agg statement. Pivotal passes each listed column as a pandas Series to the function.

python from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

with predictions as model_scores
    group by year
        agg :r2_score actual predicted as r2

Custom aggregations also work without group by:

with predictions as overall_score
    agg :r2_score actual predicted as r2

Bracket syntax supports keyword arguments:

with predictions as model_scores
    group by year
        agg :my_metric(actual, predicted, squared=False, threshold=:cutoff) as score

Use spaces between input columns in the space form. Commas continue to separate aggregation items outside brackets, so custom functions do not use the multi-column shorthand form.

Polars supports custom Python aggregations by using a pandas fallback for that aggregation step, then converting the result back to Polars. DuckDB and SQL backends raise or emit an unsupported-backend message for custom aggregation functions.

docs.title: nunique — count distinct values
docs.text:
with orders as summary
    group by region
        agg nunique customer_id as unique_customers

docs.title: agg — aggregate over all rows
docs.text:
To aggregate without grouping, use agg on its own:

with sales as totals
    agg sum revenue as total, mean price as avg_price, count id as n

This produces a single-row result. The same aggregation functions are supported as with group by.

The multi-column shorthand also works here:

with sales as averages
    agg mean price, cost, margin

docs.title: Example: full summary table
docs.text:
with orders as sales_summary
    filter status == "complete"
    group by region, category
        agg sum revenue as total, mean revenue as avg, count id as n, nunique customer_id as customers
    sort total desc

docs.title: Merge and Concatenate
docs.text: The merge statement joins two tables. The active table is the left table; the named table is the right table.

docs.title: Basic merge (inner join)
docs.text:
with sales as enriched
    merge customers on customer_id

Keeps only rows where customer_id exists in both tables.

docs.title: Join types
docs.text:
Prefix the merge with the join type:

with sales as enriched
    left merge customers on customer_id

with sales as enriched
    right merge customers on customer_id

with sales as enriched
    inner merge customers on customer_id

with sales as enriched
    outer merge customers on customer_id
Type Behaviour (none) Inner join — only matching rows left All rows from left, matched rows from right right All rows from right, matched rows from left inner Same as default — only matching rows outer All rows from both tables

docs.title: Single key
docs.text:
with sales as result
    left merge customers on customer_id

docs.title: Multiple keys
docs.text:
with orders as result
    left merge inventory on product_id, warehouse_id

docs.title: Different key names
docs.text:
When the join columns have different names in each table:

with sales as result
    left merge customers
        left_on id
        right_on customer_id

docs.title: Handling duplicate column names
docs.text:
When both tables have columns with the same name (other than the join key), suffixes are added automatically. Customise them:

with sales as result
    left merge targets on region, category
        suffixes ["_actual", "_target"]

docs.title: Example: enriching a fact table
docs.text:
load "orders.csv" as orders
load "customers.csv" as customers
load "products.csv" as products

with orders as enriched
    left merge customers on customer_id
    left merge products on product_id
    filter status == "complete"
    select order_id, date, customer_name, product_name, amount

docs.title: concat — stack tables vertically
docs.text:
Append rows from another table onto the active table:

with jan_sales as all_sales
    concat feb_sales

with q1 as all_sales
    concat q2, q3, q4

Both tables must have compatible columns. Extra columns in either table will be filled with null for the rows where they are absent.

docs.title: intersect — keep only common rows
docs.text:
Keep rows that appear in both the active table and the named table (set intersection):

with all_customers as common
    intersect active_customers

Duplicate rows are removed from the result.

docs.title: exclude — remove rows present in another table
docs.text:
Remove rows from the active table that appear in the named table (set difference):

with all_customers as new_customers
    exclude existing_customers

with leads as unmatched
    exclude converted, disqualified

Duplicate rows are removed before the comparison.

docs.title: fillna — fill missing values
docs.text: Replace null / NaN values with a constant.

docs.title: Fill all columns
docs.text:
with raw as clean
    fillna 0

with raw as clean
    fillna "unknown"

docs.title: Fill specific columns
docs.text:
Use an indented block to fill different columns with different values:

with raw as clean
    fillna
        price = 0
        name = "unknown"
        region = "N/A"

Or use comma-separated syntax:

with raw as clean
    fillna price 0, name "unknown", region "N/A"

Unquoted per-column fill values are column references:

with sales
    med_rev = median(revenue)
        by product
    fillna revenue med_rev

Only the listed columns are filled. All other columns are unchanged.

docs.title: Drop rows with any missing value
docs.text:
with raw as complete
    dropna

docs.title: Drop rows where specific columns are missing
docs.text:
Only drop a row if any of the listed columns are null:

with raw as complete
    dropna price, quantity

with raw as complete
    dropna customer_id, product_id, date

docs.title: show — display inline
docs.text:
Pivotal has three main output commands:

  • show previews the active table inline.
  • plot creates a chart from the active table.
  • table creates a formatted report table from the active table.

Use pivot plot when you want to aggregate and chart in one step without creating a separate summary table.

Display the current state of the active table inline in the notebook or terminal output.

with sales
    filter price > 100
    show

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
show          # full table
show head     # first 5 rows
show summary  # descriptive statistics (like df.describe())
show shape    # row and column counts
show columns  # column names

show can appear mid-pipeline — it displays the table at that point without interrupting subsequent operations:

with sales
    filter status == "active"
    show head              # peek at filtered data
    group by region
        agg sum revenue as total
    show                   # display final summary

docs.title: plot — create a chart
docs.text: Create a matplotlib chart from the active table.

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text:
with summary
    plot <chart_name>
        kind <chart_type>
        x <col>
        y <col>
        title "<title>"

plot uses the current active table as its source, so it fits naturally after group by, pivot, select, or other reshaping steps.

docs.title: Shorthand kind
docs.text:
The chart type can be specified directly after plot:

with summary
    plot bar revenue_chart
        x category
        y total
        title "Revenue by Category"

docs.title: Chart types
docs.text: Type Description bar Vertical bar chart line Line chart scatter Scatter plot hist Histogram box Box plot area Area chart

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Description kind "<type>" Chart type x <col> X-axis column y <col> Y-axis column (or multiple: y col1, col2) title "<text>" Chart title legend <true/false> Show/hide legend c <col> Colour-by column (scatter) colormap "<name>" Matplotlib colormap name by <col> Create faceted subplots by this column cols <n> Number of columns in faceted layout style "<file>" Path to a matplotlib style file show Render inline (in addition to viewer)

Labels can be supplied after a plotted value:

with summary
    plot line sales_chart
        x month "Month"
        y revenue "Revenue"

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
with trends
    plot line price_trend
        x date
        y price
        title "Price Over Time"
        legend False

with raw
    plot scatter price_qty
        x price
        y quantity
        c category
        colormap "viridis"
        title "Price vs Quantity"

with sales
    plot bar regional_chart
        x category
        y revenue
        by region
        cols 2
        title "Revenue by Category and Region"

docs.title: pivot plot — chart with inline aggregation
docs.text: pivot plot groups and aggregates the source table then plots the result directly, without producing a separate summary table. The y line takes one or more func col pairs separated by commas, allowing different aggregation functions per column.

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text:
with sales
    pivot plot bar revenue_chart
        x region
        y sum amount

docs.title: Multiple y columns (different funcs per column)
docs.text:
with matches
    pivot plot line season_chart
        x season
        y mean home_team_goal, mean away_team_goal "Goals"

docs.title: With filter
docs.text:
Place a filter statement before pivot plot to pre-filter the source data:

with sales
    filter year > 2020
    pivot plot bar recent_chart
        x category
        y sum revenue, mean price

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Description x <col> X-axis (group-by) column y <func> <col>, ... One or more func col pairs; optional label string at end by <col> Facet into subplots by this column cols <n> Number of columns in faceted layout (default 2) canvas <size> Figure canvas size show Render inline in addition to viewer

Aggregation functions: mean sum count min max median

docs.title: table — publication-ready table
docs.text: Create a formatted table using Great Tables. Requires pip install pivotal[tables].

docs.title: Basic table
docs.text:
with results
    table summary
        title "Sales Summary"
        format number 2

docs.title: Full options
docs.text:
with results
    table report
        title "Season Results"
        subtitle "All matches, 2023–24"
        font size 11
        font "Georgia"
        stub team, division "Club"
        spanner goals, win_rate "Performance"
        spanner revenue "Financials"
        label goals as "Goals Scored", win_rate as "Win %"
        format number 1
        format revenue as currency GBP
        format win_rate as percent 1
        summary sum as "Total", mean as "Average"
        stripe
        canvas a4
        style "my_table_style.py"
        show

docs.title: Options reference
docs.text:
Title and layout

Option Description title "<text>" Table title subtitle "<text>" Table subtitle canvas <size> Page size: a4, a4_landscape, a3, a3_landscape, letter, slide stripe Alternating row shading

Font

font size 11          # font size in pt
font "Georgia"        # font family

Stub (row labels)

The stub is the leftmost identifying column(s):

stub product                     # single column
stub product "Product"           # with custom header label
stub product, category           # column + group-by
stub product, category "Item"    # all three

Spanners (column groups)

Group columns under a shared header:

spanner price, quantity "Metrics"
spanner revenue, cost, profit "Financials"
auto spanner    # infer from MultiIndex column names

Column labels

label goals as "Goals Scored", win_rate as "Win %", revenue as "Revenue (£)"

Formatting

format number 2           # all numeric cols, 2 decimal places
format integer            # all numeric cols, no decimals
format col as number 2    # specific column
format col as currency GBP
format col as percent 1
format col as date

Summary rows

summary sum                          # one "Total" row
summary sum as "Total"               # explicit label
summary sum as "Total", mean as "Avg"  # multiple summary rows

Inline display

table my_table
    title "Results"
    show    # render inline in notebook

docs.title: Pipeline Control: Checks, Loops, and Functions
docs.text: These commands make pipelines safer and more reusable. assert and check validate assumptions, for repeats column-oriented work, and function packages a pipeline pattern for reuse.

docs.title: Assertions and Checks
docs.text:
assert and check validate the active table without changing its rows or columns.

Use assert when bad data should stop the pipeline:

with orders
    assert order_id unique
    assert customer_id not null
    assert status in ["open", "closed", "cancelled"]

Use check when bad data should warn but allow the pipeline to continue:

with orders
    check amount >= 0
    check shipped_at not null

assert and check accept the same condition syntax as filter:

with sales
    assert amount >= 0
    check region not in ["test", "sandbox"]

They also support shorthand rules for uniqueness and missing values:

with orders
    assert order_id, line_id unique
    check customer_id not null

The pandas, Polars, and DuckDB backends evaluate data-quality commands at runtime. The SQL CTE backend emits skipped comments for them because plain SQL export cannot raise Python exceptions or emit Python warnings.

docs.title: Column Loops
docs.text:
Use a for block to apply the same column-oriented operation across several columns:

with sales
    for col in price, cost, revenue
        col = col / cpi

The loop variable is a placeholder for each listed column. Only exact bare identifier matches are replaced, so a loop variable named x does not alter a column named colx.

Named Pivotal lists can provide the loop columns:

list money_cols = price, cost, revenue

with sales
    for col in money_cols
        cast col as float

Python list variables can also provide loop columns at runtime:

with sales
    for col in :money_cols
        fillna col 0

Python-list loops are not supported by the plain SQL backend because SQL export needs concrete column names.

Loop assignment targets can build new names with string suffixes or prefixes:

with sales
    for col in price, cost, revenue
        col + "_real" = col / cpi

Column loops support assignment, cast, fillna, drop, dropna, round, and window functions such as rank, lag, lead, cumsum, cummean, cummin, cummax, and rolling.

docs.title: Pipeline Functions
docs.text:
Use function to define a reusable non-recursive pipeline. Functions are expanded before validation and backend code generation, so they behave like compile-time pipeline macros:

list money_cols = price, cost, revenue

function clean_sales(input, output, cols, min_amount=0)
    with input as output
        dropna cols
        for col in cols
            cast col as float
        filter price >= min_amount
    return output

clean_sales(sales_raw, sales_clean, money_cols, min_amount=10)

Function calls use parentheses. Inline list arguments use round brackets:

clean_sales(sales_raw, sales_clean, (price, cost, revenue))

Keyword arguments and Python runtime values are supported:

clean_sales(sales_raw, sales_clean, money_cols, min_amount=:threshold)

return is optional. It has no effect during normal Pivotal execution, but records which output table should be returned when Pivotal functions are exposed through a Python-callable API:

import pivotal

funcs = pivotal.load_functions("transforms.pivotal")
sales_clean = funcs.clean_sales(
    sales_raw,
    cols=["price", "cost", "revenue"],
    min_amount=10,
)

docs.title: Python Integration
docs.text: Pivotal is designed to be embedded in Python. When its built-in operations are not enough, you can drop into Python directly.

docs.title: Single-line Python statements
docs.text:
For a single Python statement, write it on the same line as python — no end required:

with sales
    python sales["price"] = sales["price"].str.replace("$", "").astype(float)
    python sales = sales.dropna(subset=["amount"])

This is convenient for quick one-liner transformations without the overhead of a full block.

docs.title: python...end blocks
docs.text:
Embed arbitrary Python code in a Pivotal script. The block's contents are executed in the same namespace as the rest of the script, so tables defined in Pivotal are available as Python variables and vice versa.

python
    import numpy as np

    def clean_price(s):
        return s.str.replace("$", "").astype(float)

    def winsorize(df, col, lo=0.05, hi=0.95):
        low = df[col].quantile(lo)
        high = df[col].quantile(hi)
        df[col] = df[col].clip(low, high)
        return df
end

with sales
    price = :clean_price(price)

docs.title: In Jupyter notebooks
docs.text:
In a %%pivotal cell, python...end blocks can reference any variable from the notebook kernel:

# Python cell
threshold = 1000

%%pivotal
python
    filtered = sales[sales["amount"] > threshold]
end

docs.title: In .pivotal files
docs.text:
python...end blocks run in the file's execution namespace. Tables created before the block are available:

load "file.csv" as data

python
    # data is available as a pandas DataFrame
    print(data.dtypes)
    data["clean"] = data["raw"].str.strip()
end

docs.title: User-defined functions
docs.text:
Define Python functions in a python...end block and call them in column expressions with ::

python
    def clean_price(s):
        return s.str.replace("$", "").astype(float)

    def initials(s):
        return s.str[0].str.upper()
end

with sales
    price = :clean_price(price)
    abbr = :initials(name)

The : prefix marks the function as a Python runtime callable. Bare calls such as upper(name) are reserved for Pivotal built-ins or backend-native functions.

docs.title: apply — apply a Python function to a table
docs.text:
Apply a Python function that takes a DataFrame and returns a DataFrame:

python
    def remove_outliers(df):
        lo = df["price"].quantile(0.05)
        hi = df["price"].quantile(0.95)
        return df[df["price"].between(lo, hi)]

    def normalise(df):
        df["amount"] = (df["amount"] - df["amount"].mean()) / df["amount"].std()
        return df
end

with sales
    apply :remove_outliers

with sales
    apply :normalise
    group by category
        agg mean amount as avg_z_score

The : prefix marks the function as a Python runtime callable. The function receives the active DataFrame and must return a DataFrame.

docs.title: Python variable references
docs.text:
Prefix any Python variable name with : to use its value inline in Pivotal expressions:

min_date = "2024-01-01"
regions = ["North", "South"]
path = "data/sales.csv"

load :path as sales

with sales as filtered
    filter date >= :min_date
    filter region in :regions

This works with:

  • Filter conditions
  • Load paths
  • Column values in expressions (constants)
  • Lists in in / not in filters

docs.title: Working with .py and .pivotal files
docs.text: For larger projects — or when working in an editor like VS Code — it's natural to split Python logic into a separate .py file and import it into your .pivotal script. Because python executes any valid Python statement, standard imports work as-is.

docs.title: Importing a Python module
docs.text:
python from myscript import clean_price

with sales
    price = :clean_price(price)

Or use from ... import * to bring everything into the shared namespace:

python from myscript import *

with sales
    price = :clean_price(price)

docs.title: VS Code workflow
docs.text:
Keep a .py file and a .pivotal file side by side. Import the .py file at the top of your script to connect them.

project/
├── transforms.py     # Python functions, full IDE support
└── pipeline.pivotal  # Data pipeline that imports transforms.py

# transforms.py
import pandas as pd

def clean_price(s):
    return s.str.replace("$", "").astype(float)

def flag_outliers(df, col, threshold=3.0):
    z = (df[col] - df[col].mean()) / df[col].std()
    df["is_outlier"] = z.abs() > threshold
    return df

# pipeline.pivotal
python from transforms import *

load "sales.csv" as sales

with sales
    price = :clean_price(price)
    apply :flag_outliers

docs.title: Data science pipeline pattern
docs.text:
A common pattern is to alternate between Pivotal and Python: use Pivotal for data loading and wrangling, Python for analysis or modelling, then Pivotal again for result processing. 

raw_data.csv
    └── pipeline.pivotal   (load, clean, filter)
            └── analysis.py        (model, stats)
                    └── pipeline.pivotal   (aggregate, format results)


# analysis.py
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import numpy as np

def fit_model(df):
    X = df[["price", "quantity"]].values
    y = df["revenue"].values
    model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
    df["predicted"] = model.predict(X)
    df["residual"] = y - df["predicted"]
    return df

python from analysis import *

load "sales.csv" as sales

with sales
    filter region == "North"
    apply :fit_model

with sales as summary
    group by category
        agg mean residual as avg_residual
        agg mean predicted as avg_predicted

docs.title: Accessing results in Python
docs.text:
After running Pivotal code, tables are available as Python variables in the same namespace:

from pivotal import DSLParser

parser = DSLParser()
parser.execute("""
with sales as summary
    group by region
        agg sum revenue as total
""")

# Access the result
summary_df = parser.namespace['summary']
print(summary_df)

In Jupyter, tables are available directly in the next cell:

%%pivotal
with sales as summary
    group by region
        agg sum revenue as total

# Next Python cell
print(summary)  # available as a regular pandas DataFrame

docs.title: pivot — wide format
docs.text: Pivot a long table into wide format by spreading a column's values across multiple columns.

docs.title: Minimal pivot
docs.text:
with sales as pivot_table
    pivot
        rows product
        cols region
        agg sum amount

This creates a table where each unique value of region becomes a column, and each row is a product, with sum(amount) as the values.

docs.title: Multiple aggregations
docs.text:
with sales as summary
    pivot
        rows category
        cols quarter
        agg sum revenue, mean quantity

docs.title: Multiple row and column dimensions
docs.text:
with sales as detailed
    pivot
        rows product, category
        cols region, quarter
        agg sum sales, mean profit

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Description agg <fn> <col> Aggregation function and value column rows <cols> Columns to use as row index cols <cols> Column whose values become column headers

docs.title: unpivot — long format
docs.text: Convert wide-format data (multiple value columns) to long format (single value column with a variable identifier).

docs.title: Basic unpivot
docs.text:
Specify the ID column(s) to keep fixed:

with monthly_sales as long
    unpivot
        id region

All other columns become rows, with a generated variable and value column.

docs.title: Specify value columns
docs.text:
with monthly_sales as long
    unpivot
        id region
        cols jan, feb, mar, apr

Columns not listed in id or cols are dropped.

docs.title: Custom column names
docs.text:
with monthly_sales as long
    unpivot
        id region
        cols jan, feb, mar
        variable "month"
        value "amount"

docs.title: Multiple ID columns
docs.text:
with sales as long
    unpivot
        id region, year
        cols q1, q2, q3, q4
        variable "quarter"
        value "revenue"
Option Description id <cols> Columns to keep as identifiers (required) cols <cols> Columns to unpivot (optional; default = all non-id columns) variable "name" Name for the variable column (default "variable") value "name" Name for the value column (default "value")

docs.title: Save a table to a file
docs.text:
save sales as "outputs/sales.csv"
save summary as "outputs/summary.parquet"

The file format is inferred from the destination suffix. Pandas supports CSV, Parquet, JSON Lines, Feather, Excel, and pickle. Polars and DuckDB support the formats available through their backends.

Spark DataFrames can also write Delta destinations:

save sales as "dbfs:/mnt/results/sales.delta"

docs.title: Save a managed table
docs.text:
save sales as table "main.analytics.sales"

Managed table saves use the active backend. Spark DataFrames use saveAsTable; DuckDB and SQL compilation use CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE.

docs.title: Save a data package
docs.text:
save package as "outputs/my_analysis"

This saves all tables, charts, rendered tables, and Pivotal parameters in the current session.

save package as "~/projects/output/my_analysis"
    format parquet
    chart_format svg
    include sales, summary, chart1
    exclude raw, debug_plot
Option Description format <fmt> Table format: csv (default) or parquet chart_format <fmt> Chart image format: png (default) or svg include <names> Comma-separated list of objects to include exclude <names> Comma-separated list of objects to exclude

The earlier save "<package_name>" form remains supported for compatibility, but new code should use save package as "<path>".

docs.title: Loading a saved package
docs.text:
python import pivotal; _pivotal_pkg = pivotal.Package.open("my_analysis")

Then load package tables from Python:

tables = _pivotal_pkg.load_all()
sales = _pivotal_pkg.load_table("sales")

docs.title: delete - remove a table
docs.text:
Remove a table from the current session to free memory:

delete raw_import
delete scratch

In Jupyter, this is equivalent to del raw_import in Python.

docs.title: select — keep columns
docs.text:
Keep only the specified columns, in the given order:

with customers as lean
    select customer_id, name, email

with sales as report
    select product, region, revenue, date

Use a trailing \ to continue a long statement:

with sales as report
    select product, region, revenue, \
        quantity, customer_id, date

Keep columns whose names match a regex pattern:

with metrics as rates
    select matches "_rate$"

docs.title: drop — remove columns
docs.text:
Remove specific columns, keep everything else:

with raw as clean
    drop internal_id, debug_flag, temp_col

Remove columns whose names match a regex pattern:

with raw as clean
    drop matches "^temp_"

docs.title: Deduplicate on all columns
docs.text:
Remove rows where every column is identical to another row:

with sales as unique
    distinct

docs.title: Deduplicate on specific columns
docs.text:
Keep the first occurrence for each unique combination of the specified columns:

with sales as unique_products
    distinct product, category

Note

When specific columns are provided, only those columns are kept in the result. If you want to deduplicate based on certain columns but keep all columns, combine with a merge or use apply with a Python function.

docs.title: rename — rename columns
docs.text:
with sales as renamed
    rename product as item, quantity as qty, unit_price as price

Multiple renames in one statement, separated by commas.

docs.title: sort — sort rows
docs.text: Sort the table by one or more columns.

docs.title: Single column
docs.text:
with sales
    sort revenue

Default order is ascending. Specify explicitly:

with sales
    sort revenue asc
with sales
    sort revenue desc

docs.title: Multiple columns
docs.text:
Separate columns with commas:

with sales
    sort category asc, revenue desc
    sort region asc, date asc, amount desc

Each column can have its own direction.

docs.title: Column Expressions
docs.text: Create new columns or modify existing ones by writing column_name = expression indented under the with statement.

docs.title: Simple expressions
docs.text:
with sales
    revenue = price * quantity
    margin = (revenue - cost) / revenue
    tax = revenue * 0.1

Any arithmetic expression is valid: +, -, *, /, ** (power).

docs.title: Python runtime functions
docs.text:
Python functions in the runtime namespace use : in column expressions:

python
    def clean_price(s):
        return s.str.replace("$", "").astype(float)
end

with sales
    price = :clean_price(price)

Bare function calls are for Pivotal built-ins such as upper(name) or backend-native functions. Use :my_func(col) when calling Python.

docs.title: Column loops
docs.text: Column loops are covered with checks and pipeline functions in Pipeline Control.

docs.title: String functions
docs.text:
Function Description upper(col) Uppercase lower(col) Lowercase trim(col) Strip leading/trailing whitespace ltrim(col) Strip leading whitespace rtrim(col) Strip trailing whitespace left(col, n) First n characters right(col, n) Last n characters substr(col, start, length) Substring len(col) String length replace(col, old, new) Replace substring regex_extract(col, pattern) Extract first regex match regex_extract(col, pattern, group) Extract regex capture group regex_replace(col, pattern, replacement) Replace regex matches 
with products
    name = upper(name)
    code = left(sku, 4)
    slug = lower(trim(name))
    abbr = substr(code, 1, 3)
    n = len(description)
    clean = replace(notes, "N/A", "")
    postcode = regex_extract(address, "\\b\\d{4}\\b")
    clean_phone = regex_replace(phone, "[^0-9]", "")

Regex patterns use normal Pivotal strings. Escape backslashes inside quoted patterns, for example "\\b\\d{4}\\b" for a four-digit postcode on a word boundary.

String concatenation with +:

with contacts
    full_name = last_name + ", " + first_name
    label = code + "-" + region

Nesting is supported:

with products
    abbr = upper(left(name, 3))

docs.title: Date functions
docs.text:
Extract components from date/datetime columns or perform date arithmetic:

Function Description year(col) Year as integer month(col) Month (1–12) day(col) Day of month quarter(col) Quarter (1–4) dayofweek(col) Day of week (0=Monday in pandas, 1=Monday in Polars) hour(col) Hour (0–23) minute(col) Minute (0–59) date_format(col, fmt) Format as string, e.g. "%b %Y" → "Mar 2024" to_date(col) Parse a string column to date/datetime date_diff(end_col, start_col) Difference in days (integer) date_add(col, n) Add n days to a date column 
with sales
    yr       = year(order_date)
    mo       = month(order_date)
    quarter  = quarter(order_date)
    label    = date_format(order_date, "%b %Y")
    days_open = date_diff(close_date, open_date)
    due_date  = date_add(order_date, 30)

Tip: to filter or group by a date part, create the column first, then use it:

with sales as monthly
    yr = year(order_date)
    mo = month(order_date)
    filter yr == 2024
    group by yr, mo
        agg sum amount as total

docs.title: Type casting
docs.text:
Convert column data types using cast ... as <type>:

with sales
    cast price as float            # coerce — bad values become NaN/null
    cast qty as int
    cast created_at as datetime
    cast price, cost as float      # multiple columns in one statement
    cast price as float strict     # strict — raises error on bad values

Types: int / integer float string / str bool / boolean datetime

Inline cast inside an expression:

with sales
    price = float(price)
    label = str(code)
    ts    = datetime(ts_col)

docs.title: Rounding
docs.text:
Round numeric columns with round:

with sales
    round revenue 2 as revenue_rounded
    round price, cost, margin 3

Use as with one source column to create a new rounded column. Omit as to round one or more columns in place.

docs.title: Aggregate functions in expressions
docs.text:
Use aggregate functions to compute values relative to the whole table:

Function Description sum(col) Total mean(col) Average std(col) Standard deviation min(col) Minimum max(col) Maximum count(col) Count 
with sales
    pct_of_total = amount / sum(amount)
    z_score = (amount - mean(amount)) / std(amount)

Windowed aggregates — compute the aggregate within groups using by:

with sales
    pct_of_region = amount / sum(amount)
        by region

    regional_z = (amount - mean(amount)) / std(amount)
        by region, category

docs.title: Conditional assignment — where
docs.text:
Create a column with different values depending on a condition:

with sales
    discounted_price = price * 0.9
        where category == "clearance"

else is optional. Without it, rows where the condition is false receive null / NaN. Use else to provide a default:

with sales
    discounted_price = price * 0.9
        where category == "clearance"
        else price

docs.title: Multi-case assignment
docs.text:
Test multiple conditions in order; use explicit else for the default:

with sales
    tier =
        where amount > 500; "Gold"
        where amount > 100; "Silver"
        else "Bronze"

with products
    price_band =
        where price > 1000; "premium"
        where price > 200;  "mid"
        else "budget"

with sales
    adjusted =
        where amount > 500; amount * 2
        where amount > 100; amount * 1.5
        else amount

The conditions are evaluated in order; the first match wins. The else line is the default value.

map is also accepted as an alias for where in this form. It behaves the same way and is mainly intended as a friendlier keyword for exact remapping examples and AI-generated code.

docs.title: Values: Scalars, Dicts, and Lists
docs.text:
Use native Pivotal values when you want reusable constants, column groups, filter lists, or configuration that should be understood before backend code is generated.

Native values persist in the Python namespace in notebooks and %%pivotal cells, so you can also refer to them later with : runtime references. The native form is usually better inside Pivotal code because Pivotal can resolve it during validation and SQL export when the value is known.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
Use list for reusable lists of columns or literal values:

list money_cols = price, cost, revenue
list regions = "AU", "NZ", "US"
list limits = -5, 5

Lists can be used anywhere Pivotal expects a concrete list of columns, tables, or literal values:

with sales
    select product, money_cols
    filter region in regions
    filter zscore > limits[0] and zscore < limits[1]

Lists can also drive column loops:

with sales
    for col in money_cols
        col = col / cpi

docs.title: Scalars
docs.text:
Use scalar for a reusable single value:

scalar gst = 0.1
scalar min_amount = 10

with sales
    tax = price * gst
    filter amount >= min_amount

Scalar values may be numbers, booleans, strings, identifiers, paths, or Python runtime references:

scalar threshold = :notebook_threshold

docs.title: Dicts
docs.text:
Use dict for nested configuration:

dict config
    thresholds
        low = -5
        high = 5
    columns
        money = price, cost, revenue
    labels
        AU = "Australia"
        NZ = "New Zealand"
    class_names
        1 = "1st"
        2 = "2nd"

with sales
    filter zscore > config.thresholds.low and zscore < config.thresholds.high
    select product, config.columns.money
    region_name = config.labels.AU

Dictionary entries can use either = or : for values:

dict config
    thresholds
        low: -5
        high: 5

Keys can be identifiers, quoted strings, or numbers. Numeric keys in inline dictionaries are stored as string keys:

dict class_names
    1 = "1st"
    2 = "2nd"
    3 = "3rd"

Values separated by commas become lists:

dict config
    columns
        money = price, cost, revenue

docs.title: Loading Dicts
docs.text:
Load configuration from JSON or YAML by file extension:

dict config from "config.json"
dict labels from "labels.yml"

Bind an existing Python dictionary when it is already available in the runtime namespace:

dict config = :python_config

with sales
    filter amount < config.thresholds.high

YAML loading requires PyYAML to be installed.

docs.title: Native Values and :pythonvar
docs.text:
Native values and :pythonvar references overlap, but they are useful in different places.

Use native list, scalar, and dict definitions when the value is part of the Pivotal pipeline:

list money_cols = price, cost
scalar cutoff = 100

with sales
    select region, money_cols
    filter amount > cutoff

Use : references when the value is owned by surrounding Python code:

money_cols = ["price", "cost"]
cutoff = 100

with sales
    select :money_cols
    filter amount > :cutoff

Once a native value has been defined, it also exists in the Python namespace, so :money_cols or :config["thresholds"]["high"] can work in later cells. For Pivotal expressions, prefer native lookup such as money_cols, config.thresholds.high, and limits[0] when possible.

docs.title: Window Functions
docs.text: Window functions compute values across a sliding window or partition of rows, without collapsing the table. All window functions are written under the with statement.

docs.title: rank — ranking
docs.text: Rank rows by a column value.

docs.title: Basic rank
docs.text:
with sales
    rank amount desc as sales_rank

docs.title: Ascending rank
docs.text:
with sales
    rank amount asc as rank_asc

docs.title: Percentile rank
docs.text:
Returns a value between 0 and 1:

with sales
    rank amount pct as pct_rank

docs.title: Partitioned rank (rank within groups)
docs.text:
Use by to rank within groups:

with sales
    rank amount desc as regional_rank
        by region

with sales
    rank amount desc as cat_rank
        by region, category

docs.title: lag / lead — shifted values
docs.text: Access values from a previous (lag) or future (lead) row.

docs.title: Basic lag
docs.text:
with sales
    lag amount 1 as prev_amount
        order date

The order clause specifies which column defines row order. It is required.

docs.title: Lead
docs.text:
with sales
    lead amount 1 as next_amount
        order date

docs.title: With partition
docs.text:
with sales
    lag amount 1 as prev_regional_amount
        by region
        order date

docs.title: Larger offsets
docs.text:
with sales
    lag amount 3 as amount_3_periods_ago
        order date

docs.title: Cumulative statistics
docs.text:
Compute running totals, averages, min, and max.

Statement Description cumsum <col> as <name> Running sum cummean <col> as <name> Running average cummin <col> as <name> Running minimum cummax <col> as <name> Running maximum

The order clause specifies row order and is required. Use by for partitioned cumulation.

with sales
    cumsum amount as running_total
        order date

with sales
    cummean amount as running_avg
        order date

with sales
    cummin amount as running_min
        by region
        order date

with sales
    cummax amount as running_max
        by region
        order date

docs.title: Partitioned cumulation
docs.text:
with sales
    cumsum amount as regional_running_total
        by region
        order date

docs.title: rolling — rolling window statistics
docs.text:
Compute statistics over a sliding window of N rows.

with sales
    rolling mean amount 7 as rolling_7d_avg
        order date

docs.title: Rolling functions
docs.text: Function Description rolling mean <col> <n> Rolling average rolling sum <col> <n> Rolling sum rolling std <col> <n> Rolling standard deviation rolling min <col> <n> Rolling minimum rolling max <col> <n> Rolling maximum

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
with sales
    rolling mean amount 4 as rolling_avg
        by region     # compute within groups
        order date    # required: defines row order
        min_periods 1 # optional: allow early rows before a full window

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
with daily_sales
    rolling sum revenue 7 as weekly_revenue
        order date

with daily_sales
    rolling mean revenue 30 as monthly_avg
        order date

with regional_sales
    rolling sum revenue 4 as quarterly_rolling
        by region
        order date
